title: Improve Listening By Softening Your Voice
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Michael Linsin argues that most teachers talk too loudly because they believe it shows they mean it, earns respect and makes students listen, and that all three beliefs are false. A raised voice means students need not stop, look or lean in, so they fidget and whisper while the sound washes over them, and eventually tune the teacher out. Softening the voice, just enough for the farthest student to hear, makes students incline toward the teacher, draw their eyes to them and become receptive. A calm voice also communicates respect and trust in students' ability to listen, calms nervous energy in the room, and signals that the teacher is in control. Because students mirror what teachers do, a quieter teacher tends to produce quieter students. He allows volume and passion for presenting lessons or playing games, but says that for directions and behavior issues the teacher should stand still, make eye contact and speak softly.
points: Shouting gives students no reason to stop or look at the teacher, and over time the volume becomes a nuisance they tune out.
Lowering the voice to just reach the farthest student pulls students' attention toward the teacher, so they lean in and listen.
A calm voice conveys respect and trust, so students tend to return the favor by doing what is asked.
Because students copy teachers' behavior, a softer teacher voice leads to students modulating their own volume.
Save passion and volume for teaching moments, and use a soft, steady voice with eye contact for directions and behavior.
quotes: When you bellow out directions, your students don’t have to stop what they’re doing. They don’t have to look at you or become still.

But when you soften your voice—just enough so students farthest from you are able to hear—they naturally begin to listen better. They incline their body toward you. Their eyes draw to you. They become receptive.
A calm and pleasant voice also goes down smoother. It sounds polite and communicates that you believe in your students and their ability to listen.
Like all of us, students appreciate being spoken to with respect. They like being trusted with the information you give them and not bludgeoned over the head with it.
Furthermore, speaking softly has a calming effect. Just opening your mouth releases excitability and nervous tension—which is most often caused by loud, stressed-out, and fast-moving teachers.
It shows you’re in control and know what you’re doing. This is a soothing notion to students, freeing them to concentrate on their learning.
Because what you do is more influential than what you say, when you quiet your voice, your students will do the same. They’ll too modulate to a gentler volume.
But when you’re giving directions, handling behavior issues, and otherwise attending to day-to-day operations, it’s best to dial it down.
